title: Disk throughput is low while utilization and I/O wait are high
body: I expect disk utilization to be normal, but `mc support top disk` shows most of my MinIO data disks at 100% utilization even though each disk is reading only about 0.02–0.09 MiB/s and writing about 1–2 MiB/s. Await times reach hundreds of milliseconds. `iotop` shows low aggregate throughput but very high I/O wait for MinIO threads and `xfsaild`. MinIO is running as `minio server --console-address :30091 /data/minio-data-{1...12}`.

symptoms_visible: Most of my MinIO data disks show 100% utilization while each is transferring only around 1–2 MiB/s.
Disk await times reach hundreds of milliseconds, and MinIO and xfsaild threads spend a lot of time waiting for I/O.
N0.label: N0 high disk utilization reported

symptoms_visible: The disks remain highly utilized while the client uploads 10 to 20 objects per second, with each object around 500 KB.
N1.label: N1 small-object workload established

symptoms_visible: The existing HDD-backed cluster still shows high utilization and long waits under the small-object upload workload.
N2.label: N2 HDD storage identified

symptoms_visible: My HDDs remain at high utilization with low bandwidth while handling many roughly 500 KB uploads.
N3.label: N3 IOPS limit diagnosed

symptoms_visible: After I applied the write-through queue setting, my CPU load average fell from about 1500 to 125.
N_terminal.label: terminal mitigation confirmed

question_patterns: What is the S3 client doing when utilization reaches 100%?
Approximately how many PUT requests are arriving per second?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: My S3 client puts about 10 to 20 objects per second.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: There are no active PUT requests when this happens; the cluster is idle.
The client puts about 15 to 25 objects per second.

edges.comment: Issue comments c0-c1, describing the reporter's S3 workload. The reporter then added the object size in c2 without another question.

question_patterns: Is this a new cluster, or did the same cluster previously perform better?
Do you have an earlier disk-I/O baseline for this deployment?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It is not a new cluster, but I hadn't paid attention to the disk I/O before, so I don't have an earlier comparison.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The same workload was much faster on these disks until a MinIO update yesterday.

question_patterns: What kind of storage devices back these data paths?
Can you identify whether these drives are HDDs or SSDs, or share the relevant lsblk output?

counterfactual_candidates.answer: They are enterprise NVMe SSDs with plenty of available IOPS.
They are 7200 RPM HDDs rather than slower archival HDDs.

edges.comment: Issue comments c5-c9, all concerning the reporter's existing cluster. Although lsblk was requested, the reporter's actual answer only identified the devices as HDDs.

solution.intent: Diagnose the low-bandwidth, high-utilization behavior as HDD IOPS saturation caused by many small object writes being expanded across a wide erasure-coded set, rather than as a bandwidth-utilization bug in MinIO.
solution.concrete_example: A roughly 500 KB object may be split into multiple data and parity fragments across the 12-drive erasure set, creating many small I/O operations plus metadata overhead. At 10–20 PUTs per second, HDDs can exhaust their IOPS while transferring only a few MiB/s, which explains 100% utilization and long await times.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the workload rate, object size, 12-drive command, HDD type, utilization, and await values. Inferring erasure-fragment I/O amplification and concluding that the HDDs have exhausted their available IOPS is engineer-side reasoning from that evidence.

edges.comment: Issue comments c7-c10 and the final closure in c17: participants diagnose an HDD IOPS ceiling. Comment c8 explains that small files spread across data and parity fragments create many operations, so HDD IOPS can saturate at low client bandwidth.

solution.intent: Use the explicitly write-through block queue mode as the tested mitigation, not write-back or fsync bypass, and verify the result on the reporter's workload while recognizing that the underlying HDD IOPS ceiling remains.
solution.concrete_example: For each actual data device, test `echo "write through" | sudo tee /sys/block/<device>/queue/write_cache`. The thread also advises disabling the drive's own cache with the appropriate hdparm setting for consistency. Do not substitute write-back or bypass fsync. Re-run the same workload and compare utilization, await, throughput, and load before treating the mitigation as successful.

edges.comment: Issue comments c11-c16: participant1 proposed write-through queue mode and disabling the physical drive cache; after the device-path syntax was corrected, the reporter tried it and reported that CPU load average fell from 1500 to 125. Comments c17-c21 briefly warn about write-back/fsync bypass and cache exhaustion, but participant3 explicitly retracts that warning after realizing the recommendation was write-through, not write-back. The final diagnosis still remains the hardware IOPS limit.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause as HDD IOPS saturation: 10–20 roughly 500 KB PUTs per second are expanded into many small data, parity, and metadata operations across the wide erasure-coded drive set, so utilization can reach 100% at low MiB/s.
The diagnosis must be grounded in the reported HDD type, small-object workload, 12-drive layout, high await times, and low per-disk throughput.

If recommending the thread's tested mitigation, it must specify write-through rather than write-back, must not recommend bypassing fsync, and should preserve consistency by addressing the drive cache as described.
Must not repeat the retracted claim that this write-through result only lasts until a newly enabled cache fills; that warning came from misreading the setting as write-back.
Must explain that the mitigation does not remove the underlying HDD IOPS ceiling and that sustained capacity ultimately requires changing the workload/layout or using storage with more IOPS.

Must ask the reporter to verify under the same workload and only treat the mitigation as successful after the observable result; in this case the reporter reported CPU load average falling from about 1500 to 125.

persona_hint.experience_level: MinIO operator comfortable running command-line monitoring tools and changing Linux block-device settings, but seeking guidance on storage behavior and cautious about settings that might reduce performance.
persona_hint.communication_style: Brief and direct; supplies requested facts in short replies, asks practical follow-up questions, and reports a clear before-and-after result enthusiastically.
